p.src: Now it is told that on that day the three advance divisions of Song Jiang’s vanguard swept across the opposing lines. Wielding broadswords and great axes, they routed Tong Guan’s entire army, scattering the troops like falling stars and drifting clouds and leaving them grievously mauled. The soldiers cast away gongs and drums, abandoned halberds and spears, and went searching for sons and fathers while calling for brothers and younger kin. More than ten thousand men and horses were lost before the army withdrew thirty li and pitched camp. From within the formation, Wu Yong sounded the gong to recall the troops and passed down an order: “We must not yet pursue and slaughter them without restraint. For now, let us merely give them a warning.” The forces of Liangshan Marsh all returned to the stronghold, where each man reported his achievements and sought his reward.

p.src: As for Tong Guan, after losing the battle and many men and horses, he promptly set up a fortified camp and settled his troops. Troubled at heart, he summoned his commanders to confer. The two generals Feng Mei and Bi Sheng said, “Grand Councillor, do not be distressed. Knowing that the imperial army was coming, these bandits arranged this formation in advance. Our army had only just arrived and knew nothing of the true situation, so we fell victim to their treacherous scheme. These mere outlaws rely only on the strength of their mountains, making a great display of troops to exaggerate their power. We were defeated because we momentarily lost the advantage of the terrain. Let us reorganize and drill our cavalry and infantry, rest for three days to restore their fighting spirit, and tend the warhorses. Three days from now we shall arrange all our officers and men in a Long Snake formation and send the infantry forward to attack. This formation is like the long snake of Mount Chang: strike its head and its tail responds; strike its tail and its head responds; strike its middle and both head and tail respond. Every part must remain continuously linked. If we stake the outcome on this one battle, we are certain to win a great victory.” Tong Guan said, “An excellent plan! It accords perfectly with my own thoughts.” He immediately issued his military orders, and the three armies were put in order and fully trained.

p.src: At the fifth watch on the third day, the food was prepared. Officers and soldiers ate their fill; the horses wore leather armor and the men iron mail. Great blades and broad axes were made ready, and bows and crossbows were strung. Truly, spears and swords streamed onward like rushing water, while men and horses sped like a driving gale. The great generals Feng Mei and Bi Sheng led the army in front, advancing in a mighty host to attack Liangshan Marsh. The eight columns divided to left and right, while three hundred armored scouts were sent ahead to reconnoiter. They returned to inform Tong Guan at headquarters: “There is not a single soldier or horse on the battlefield of the other day.” Hearing this, Tong Guan grew suspicious. He came forward in person and asked Feng Mei and Bi Sheng, “Should we withdraw?” Feng Mei replied, “Do not entertain thoughts of retreat. Let us simply press straight ahead. Once the Long Snake formation is deployed, what have we to fear?” The imperial army advanced in a long procession until it reached the edge of the marsh, yet not a single soldier or horse appeared. Across the boundless waters they saw only reeds and smoky haze. Far away, atop the stronghold by the water’s edge, an apricot-yellow banner fluttered, but otherwise there was not the slightest movement. Tong Guan, Feng Mei, and Bi Sheng reined in their horses before the vast army. Looking toward the opposite shore, they saw a small boat among the reeds. A lone man aboard wore a green bamboo-leaf hat and a green straw rain cape. Leaning sideways against the boat with his back toward the western bank, he fished alone. From across the bank, Tong Guan’s infantry called to the fisherman and asked, “Where are the bandits?” The fisherman made no reply. Tong Guan ordered his skilled archers to shoot. Two horsemen rode straight to the shoal at the water’s edge. Reining in their mounts beside the water, they drew their bows and set arrows to the strings. One aimed at the fisherman’s back and loosed with a hiss. The arrow struck squarely upon the bamboo-leaf hat with a clang, then fell into the water. The other cavalryman loosed an arrow that struck the rain cape squarely. It too rang out with a clang and dropped into the water. These two horsemen were the finest archers in Tong Guan’s army. Both were startled. They reined their horses around, returned, and bowed as they reported to Tong Guan: “Both arrows struck, but they could not pierce him. We do not know what he is wearing.” Tong Guan then detached three hundred scouting cavalrymen able to draw powerful bows. They deployed along the shoal and all shot at the fisherman together. The arrows flew in a chaotic shower, but the fisherman remained unruffled. Many arrows fell into the water, and some struck the boat; but every shaft that hit the rain cape or bamboo-leaf hat dropped harmlessly into the water.

p.src: When Tong Guan saw that the arrows could not kill him, he ordered soldiers skilled in swimming to strip off their clothes and armor, enter the water, and capture the fisherman. Before long, thirty or fifty men had plunged in and begun swimming across. Hearing the water splash astern, the fisherman knew men were approaching. Without hurry or alarm, he laid down his fishing tackle and took up the boat pole beside him. Each man who came near the boat received a single blow: some were struck on the temple, some on the crown, and some squarely in the face, and all were knocked into the water. Those behind, seeing several men sink, turned and swam back to shore to look for their clothes and armor. At the sight, Tong Guan flew into a rage and ordered five hundred soldiers into the water, commanding them to capture the fisherman without fail; any man who returned was to be cut in two with a single stroke. The five hundred soldiers stripped off their clothes and armor, raised a mighty shout, and all leapt into the water and swam across together. The fisherman turned the prow around, pointed at Tong Guan on the bank, and cursed loudly: “You traitorous minister who throws the realm into disorder, you beast who torments the people! You have come here to offer up your life, yet still you do not know that death awaits you!” Tong Guan was furious and shouted for the cavalry to loose their arrows. The fisherman laughed heartily and said, “Ah, troops have arrived over there!” Pointing with his hand, he cast aside his rain cape and bamboo-leaf hat, flipped over, and plunged beneath the water. The five hundred soldiers had just reached the boat when cries of confusion arose from the water, and they all began to sink. The fisherman was none other than Zhang Shun, the “White Streak in the Waves.” His bamboo-leaf hat was wrapped with bamboo leaves on the outside but fashioned from copper within; and beneath his rain cape was a single sheet of tempered copper, shaped like a tortoise shell. No wonder the arrows could not pierce it. Zhang Shun dived to the bottom, drew the saber at his waist, and stabbed the men one after another down the line. They sank beneath the surface as bloody water came boiling up. A few quick-witted men swam away and escaped with their lives. Tong Guan stared in stupefaction from the bank. A general beside him pointed and said, “That yellow banner on the mountaintop is waving to and fro.”

p.src: Tong Guan peered intently but could not grasp its meaning, and none of the generals knew what to make of it. Feng Mei said, “Divide the three hundred armored scouts into two companies and send them behind the mountains on either side to reconnoiter and see what is happening.” They had scarcely divided and reached the front of the mountains when a thunderous signal cannon erupted from among the reeds, sending fire and smoke swirling into confusion. The scouts from both sides galloped back together to report that an ambush force was upon them. Tong Guan received no small fright in the saddle. Feng Mei and Bi Sheng sent men to both flanks, ordering the soldiers not to stir in disorder. The hundreds of thousands of troops all drew their blades and held them ready. Mounted messengers galloped back and forth, shouting, “Anyone who flees first will be beheaded!” Thus they held the entire army in place. As Tong Guan and his generals sat their horses and watched, drums thundered behind the mountain, shaking the earth, and battle cries rose to the heavens. In an instant, a powerful body of troops swept forth, all bearing yellow banners, led by two valiant generals. And how splendidly ordered was that body of troops?

p.src: Mounted on two yellow-maned horses were two heroic chieftains: in the leading place, Zhu Tong, the Beautiful-Bearded Lord, and below him, Lei Heng, the Winged Tiger. At the head of five thousand men and horse, they charged straight at the imperial army. Tong Guan ordered his generals Feng Mei and Bi Sheng to go forward and meet the enemy. Receiving the order, the two spurred their horses, leveled their spears, and rode out from the lines, shouting abuse: “You wanton grass bandits! If you will not come and surrender now, how long do you mean to wait?” Lei Heng laughed aloud from horseback and shouted, “Fool! Death is before your very eyes, yet you do not know it! How dare you challenge me to battle?” Bi Sheng flew into a rage, spurred his horse, and thrust his spear straight at Lei Heng; Lei Heng met him with his own spear. The horses crossed, and their weapons rose together. The two generals fought for more than twenty bouts without either gaining the advantage. Seeing that Bi Sheng could not prevail after so long a fight, Feng Mei spurred forward, brandishing his saber, and went directly to his aid. At the sight, Zhu Tong gave a mighty shout, galloped forward, and swung his saber at Feng Mei. Before the battle lines, the four horses fought in two pairs. Tong Guan watched and called out praise without cease. When the fighting had carried them deep into the ravine, Zhu Tong and Lei Heng suddenly showed an opening, wheeled their horses, and fled toward their own lines. The two generals Feng Mei and Bi Sheng refused to let them go and spurred after them. The opposing army raised a great shout and fled behind the mountain. Tong Guan ordered an all-out pursuit beyond its foot, but then horns sounded together from the summit. When the generals looked up, two signal shots rose, one before them and one behind. Tong Guan realized that an ambush lay in wait. He halted his troops and ordered them not to pursue.

p.src: Then an apricot-yellow banner appeared upon the summit, embroidered with the four words “Carry Out Justice on Heaven’s Behalf.” When Tong Guan went around to look from the other side of the mountain, a cluster of multicolored embroidered banners opened upon the summit, revealing Song Jiang, the peerless hero of Yuncheng County in Shandong, known as the Guardian of Justice. Behind him stood the strategist Wu Yong, Gongsun Sheng, Hua Rong, Xu Ning, the Golden Spearmen, the Silver Spearmen, and many other heroes. Tong Guan was enraged at the sight and at once sent troops up the mountain to seize Song Jiang. The great host divided into two columns and was just about to climb the mountain when drums and music thundered from the summit, and all the heroes laughed. Tong Guan’s fury mounted. Grinding his teeth, he shouted, “How dare these bandits make sport of me! I shall capture that wretch myself.” Feng Mei remonstrated, “Grand Councillor, they must have some stratagem prepared. You must not venture personally into dangerous ground. Please withdraw the army for now. Tomorrow we may learn the truth of their strength and only then advance.” Tong Guan said, “Nonsense! Now that matters have come this far, how can we retreat? We were ordered to engage the bandits day and night. Now that the bandits are in sight, circumstances permit no retreat. …” Before he had finished speaking, shouts arose from the rear guard. A scout reported, “A body of troops has charged out from behind the mountain due west and cut the rear guard into two!” Tong Guan was greatly alarmed. Taking Feng Mei and Bi Sheng with him, he hurried back to aid the rear guard, but at the sound of drums behind the eastern mountain, another force had already come flying forth. Half bore red banners and half green banners. With two great generals at their head, five thousand troops came charging forward. p.src: The leader of the black-banner company was Huyan Zhuo of the Twin Whips, and the leader of the white-banner company was Lin Chong, the Panther Head. The two generals shouted from horseback, “Treacherous minister Tong Guan, where do you think you are fleeing? Come quickly and meet your death!” With one charge, they drove straight into the midst of the army. Duan Pengju, military superintendent of Suizhou, engaged Huyan Zhuo, while Ma Wanli, military superintendent of Ruzhou, took on Lin Chong. Ma Wanli had fought Lin Chong for only a few bouts when, finding himself no match in strength, he made ready to flee. But Lin Chong gave a great shout, throwing him into confusion, and caught him with a thrust that knocked him from his horse. When Duan Pengju saw Ma Wanli stabbed to death by Lin Chong, he lost all desire to continue fighting. He warded off Huyan Zhuo’s twin whips, abruptly wheeled his horse, and fled. Huyan Zhuo pressed after him valiantly. The two armies became entangled in a melee, while Tong Guan merely ordered his men to seize any road they could and retreat. Suddenly a mighty shouting arose before the army, and a force of infantry swept out from behind the mountain, charging straight into the heart of the encirclement. At their head were a monk and a pilgrim, leading the soldiers and shouting, “Do not let Tong Guan escape!” That monk performed neither sutras nor rites but delighted only in killing. His sobriquet was the Flowery Monk, and his full name was Lu Zhishen. That pilgrim had once slain a tiger on Jingyang Ridge. Foremost in heroism at the Water Margin stronghold, he was the famous Pilgrim Wu Song. These two cut their way into the battle lines. What was the sight like? Huyan Zhuo pressed after him valiantly. The two armies became entangled in a melee, while Tong Guan merely ordered his men to seize any road they could and retreat.
Suddenly a mighty shouting arose before the army, and a force of infantry swept out from behind the mountain, charging straight into the heart of the encirclement.
At their head were a monk and a pilgrim, leading the soldiers and shouting, “Do not let Tong Guan escape!”
That monk performed neither sutras nor rites but delighted only in killing. His sobriquet was the Flowery Monk, and his full name was Lu Zhishen.
That pilgrim had once slain a tiger on Jingyang Ridge. Foremost in heroism at the Water Margin stronghold, he was the famous Pilgrim Wu Song.
These two cut their way into the battle lines.
What was the sight like? A lyric to the tune “Moon over the West River” bears witness:

p.src: Lu Zhishen wields a single monk’s staff; Pilgrim Wu brandishes two steel sabers. The steel sabers fly, scattering fiery sparks; the monk’s staff strikes like an iron cannonball. The monk’s staff smashes open skulls; the steel sabers sever men at the waist. Neither of the two weapons shows mercy; amid a million troops their splendor is displayed.

p.src: These two fierce generals were Dong Ping, the Double-Speared General, and Suo Chao, the Impatient Vanguard. Without exchanging a word, they galloped straight at Tong Guan. Wang Yi leveled his spear and rode to meet them, but Suo Chao raised his axe and brought it down, hewing him from the saddle. Han Tianlin came to his aid, but Dong Ping killed him with a single spear thrust. Feng Mei and Bi Sheng defended Tong Guan to the death as they spurred their horses and fled for their lives. Gongs and drums sounded wildly on every side, and no one knew where the troops were coming from. Tong Guan reined in his horse on a slope and looked about. Four cavalry columns advanced from every quarter, while two infantry columns pressed in along either flank. Formed like iron hoops and open winnowing baskets, the great host of Liangshan Marsh came charging together. Tong Guan's army scattered like clouds before the wind and fell into utter confusion. As he watched, a cluster of troops emerged below the slope. From their banners he recognized Wu Bingyi, military commissioner of Chenzhou, and Li Ming, military commissioner of Xuzhou. The two led a remnant force with broken spears and shattered halberds, circling around Mount Linlang to seek shelter. When they saw the signals, they were about to climb the slope and hurriedly wheeled their troops around. Just then shouts rose beside the mountain, and another body of troops swept out in pursuit. Two identification banners fluttered, and beneath them two fierce generals, each wielding a weapon, galloped upon the imperial troops. Who were these two? A lyric to the tune “Immortal by the River” bears witness:

p.src: Long tassels on their helmets dance like flames, scattering trails of brilliant scarlet; the heroic spirit in their breasts breathes forth a rainbow. Their battle robes are cut from Sichuan brocade, their armor plated with gold and bronze. Two precious swords gleam like snowy silk; displaying their might amid the encirclement, they charge left and right and show themselves true heroes. The warrior called the Blue-Faced Beast; the brave known as the Nine-Tattooed Dragon.

p.src: These two fierce generals were Yang Zhi and Shi Jin. With two horses and two swords, they had just intercepted the officers Wu Bingyi and Li Ming and engaged them in combat. Li Ming leveled his spear, advanced, and engaged Yang Zhi. Wu Bingyi wielded a heaven-square halberd and rode against Shi Jin. The two pairs wheeled back and forth below the slope, circling round and round, each displaying the martial skill of a lifetime. Tong Guan held his horse on the slope and watched in anxious uncertainty. After the four had fought for more than thirty bouts, Wu Bingyi thrust his halberd at Shi Jin's heart. Shi Jin merely swerved, letting the weapon pass beneath his ribs. Wu Bingyi and his horse lunged too far forward; Shi Jin raised his sword and struck, and in a flash a bloodied strip of flesh was laid bare as Wu's golden helmet fell beside the horse. Wu Bingyi died below the slope. Seeing his comrade fall first, Li Ming was about to wheel his horse and flee when Yang Zhi gave a tremendous shout. It frightened him out of his wits and chilled him to the marrow, until he no longer knew which end of his spear was uppermost. Yang Zhi brought his sword down upon the crown of Li Ming's head. Li Ming dodged, and the blade struck the horse squarely on its hindquarters. The animal collapsed on its hind legs and pitched Li Ming from the saddle. He dropped his spear and was about to run, but Yang Zhi was quick: following up with another stroke, he struck him squarely. Pitiful Li Ming—a military officer for half his life, now all had dissolved into a dream of Nanke. Both imperial generals died below the slope. Yang Zhi and Shi Jin pursued and slaughtered the routed troops as easily as chopping melons and gourds.

p.src: Tong Guan, Feng Mei, and Bi Sheng watched from the slope. They dared not descend and were utterly at a loss. The three consulted together. “How can we possibly fight our way out of this?” Feng Mei said, “Set your mind at ease, Grand Marshal. I can see that a great body of imperial troops is still encamped due south. Their banners have not fallen, so they can come to our rescue. Commander Bi, remain on the hilltop and guard the Grand Marshal. I shall open a road by force, bring that army here, and escort the Grand Marshal out.” Tong Guan said, “Night is drawing near. Watch for your opportunity, go swiftly, and return soon.” Feng Mei gripped his long-shafted broadsword, galloped down the mountain, hacked open a path, and rode straight south. When he reached that force, he found Zhou Xin, military commissioner of Songzhou, who had formed his soldiers into a tight circle and was defending the heart of the battlefield to the death. Seeing Feng Mei approach, Zhou Xin admitted him into the formation and asked, “Where is the Grand Marshal?” Feng Mei replied, “He is on the slope just ahead, waiting expressly for your troops to go to his rescue and fight their way out with him. There is no time to lose. Move at once!” When Zhou Xin heard this, he ordered the command passed down: cavalry and infantry alike were to look out for one another, keep their ranks intact, and unite their strength and purpose. The two great generals led the way, and the soldiers raised battle cries as they fought toward the slope. Before they had gone the distance of an arrow's flight, a force approached obliquely from the side. Feng Mei brandished his sword and rode straight out to meet it, then recognized Duan Pengju, military commissioner of Suizhou. The three met, combined their troops, and fought their way to the foot of the slope. Bi Sheng descended the slope to meet them and brought them to Tong Guan. Together they discussed, “Would it be better to fight our way out tonight, or wait until tomorrow morning?” Feng Mei said, “The four of us will defend the Grand Marshal to the death. If we break through the encirclement tonight, we can escape these bandits.”

p.src: As night drew near, unceasing battle cries could be heard on every side, amid the wild clamor of gongs and drums. Around the second watch, under the bright stars and moon, Feng Mei took the lead. The officers clustered around Tong Guan in their midst, and all joined forces to fight their way down the slope. From all around came confused shouts: “Don't let Tong Guan escape!” The imperial troops fought desperately toward the road due south. After fighting in the melee until about the fourth watch, they finally broke out of the encirclement. On horseback, Tong Guan raised a hand to his brow and bowed in worship to Heaven, Earth, and the gods, saying, “Thank Heaven! I have escaped this terrible calamity!” He urged them onward beyond the border and fled toward Jizhou.

None can withstand his twelve-foot steel spear; astride his fleet horse, he soars through the clouds, peerless in both bearing and martial skill. Lu Junyi of Liangshan, the Jade Qilin of Hebei.

p.src: The heroic general on horseback was none other than Lu Junyi, the “Jade Qilin.” The two heroes before his horse, each wielding a broad-bladed sword, were Yang Xiong, the “Sick Guansuo,” and Shi Xiu, the “Desperate Third Son.” By the light of their torches they led more than three thousand men forward in high spirits and blocked the road. From horseback Lu Junyi shouted, “Tong Guan, why have you not dismounted and submitted to binding? What are you waiting for?” Hearing this, Tong Guan said to his men, “There are ambushers ahead and pursuers behind. What are we to do now?” Feng Mei said, “I will sacrifice my life to repay Your Excellency. All you officers, guard him closely, force a way through, and make for Jizhou. I shall remain here and hold off these bandits.” Feng Mei spurred his horse, brandished his saber, and charged straight at Lu Junyi. Their horses crossed, but before they had fought more than a few bouts, Lu Junyi made a single thrust with his spear, forced aside the great saber, and closed in. Seizing Feng Mei around the waist, he kicked his warhorse away and captured him alive. Yang Xiong and Shi Xiu came forward to support him, and all their troops swarmed in, hauling and dragging Feng Mei away. Bi Sheng, Zhou Xin, and Duan Pengju risked their lives to protect Tong Guan, cutting through the troops blocking their way as they fought and retreated. Lu Junyi pursued from behind, while Tong Guan’s routed army fled in frantic haste, like homeless curs and fish escaped from the net. At dawn they finally shook off their pursuers and headed toward Jizhou.

To slay a tiger, one must enter its deepest lair; to kill a dragon, one must descend into the abyss. The might of their hosts shakes the azure sky; living demons stand revealed before the eye.

p.src: Li Kui swung his two broad axes, Bao Xu wielded a fine sword, and Xiang Chong and Li Gun each flourished a barbarian shield to cover them. Like a ball of fire rolling over the ground, they came on and scattered the government troops in every direction. Tong Guan and his generals fought as they fled, concerned only with escaping alive. Li Kui hacked his way straight into the cavalry ranks and cut down Duan Pengju’s horse at the legs, pitching him to the ground. Following through with one axe, he split open his skull, then with another severed his throat. Plainly, Duan Pengju could not survive. Now the battered remnants of the government army were nearing Jizhou. Their helmets hung askew over their ears, their neck guards half covered their cheeks, and neither cavalry nor infantry had any strength left; men and horses alike were exhausted. Reaching a stream, the soldiers and horses went to drink. Suddenly a cannon boomed from across the stream, and arrows flew toward them like a swarm of locusts. The government troops scrambled up the bank, but a body of cavalry wheeled out from beside the woods. Who were the three heroes riding at its head?

p.src: These were Zhang Qing, the “Featherless Arrow,” together with Gong Wang and Ding Desun, leading more than three hundred cavalrymen. This troop of valiant cavalry all wore masks adorned with bronze bells and red plumes of pheasant feathers; they carried light bows, short arrows, embroidered banners, and decorated spears. With the three generals in the lead, they charged straight forward. Zhou Xin, military commissioner of Songzhou, saw that Zhang Qing had few horsemen and rode out to meet him; Bi Sheng escorted Tong Guan away. Zhou Xin galloped forward with leveled spear. Zhang Qing tucked his own spear under his left arm, raised his right hand in the pose of the Seventh Treasure-Summoning Lad, and cried, “Take that!” A single stone struck Zhou Xin squarely in the hollow of his nose, and he toppled backward from his horse. Gong Wang and Ding Desun galloped up from the sides to help, pinning his throat with their two forks. Like frost withering frontier grass and rain battering blossoms in the imperial park, Zhou Xin died beneath the horses’ hooves. Tong Guan fled for his life with Bi Sheng alone. Not daring to enter Jizhou, he gathered the remnants of his defeated army and made for the Eastern Capital through the night, collecting scattered fugitives along the road and making camp.

p.src: Song Jiang was benevolent and virtuous and had always cherished the desire to submit to the court, so he would not permit an unrestrained pursuit and slaughter. Fearing that his commanders would refuse to desist and continue chasing Tong Guan, he urgently dispatched Dai Zong with orders for all the chiefs to gather their cavalry and infantry from every route and return to the mountain stronghold to claim their rewards. Everywhere the gongs sounded the recall. The mounted generals struck their golden stirrups, the foot soldiers sang songs of victory, and in thronging ranks they all entered Liangshan Marsh and returned together to Wanzi City.

u.src: Song Jiang was benevolent and virtuous and had always cherished the desire to submit to the court, so he would not permit an unrestrained pursuit and slaughter. Fearing that his commanders would refuse to desist and continue chasing Tong Guan, he urgently dispatched Dai Zong with orders for all the chiefs to gather their cavalry and infantry from every route and return to the mountain stronghold to claim their rewards.

Everywhere the gongs sounded the recall. The mounted generals struck their golden stirrups, the foot soldiers sang songs of victory, and in thronging ranks they all entered Liangshan Marsh and returned together to Wanzi City.

p.src: Song Jiang, Wu Yong, and Gongsun Sheng reached the stronghold in the marsh first. They took their seats in the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness and ordered Pei Xuan to examine each man’s achievements and rewards. Lu Junyi brought Feng Mei, whom he had captured alive, up to the stronghold and made him kneel before the hall. Song Jiang personally untied him, invited him into the hall to take the seat of honor, and with his own hands offered him a cup, conversing with him and serving wine to calm his fright. When all the chiefs had assembled in the hall, oxen and horses were slaughtered that day, and the entire army was richly rewarded. Feng Mei was kept as a guest for two days; then saddle and horse were prepared, and he was escorted down the mountain. Feng Mei was overjoyed. Song Jiang said courteously, “General, before and after the battle we offended your dignity; I earnestly beg your forgiveness. We, Song Jiang and his companions, harbor no rebellious intent. We desire only to submit to the court and serve the country, but unjust and lawless men have driven us to this pass. I hope that when you return to court, General, you will speak kindly on our behalf and obtain deliverance for us. If one day we may again behold the light of imperial favor, we shall never forget your great kindness, in life or in death.” Feng Mei bowed in gratitude for having been spared and set out down the mountain. Song Jiang ordered men to escort him all the way beyond their territory. His return to the capital need not be related.

p.src: Song Jiang returned to the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness and again conferred with Wu Yong and the other chiefs. The strategy of ambush on ten sides used this time had been entirely devised and arranged by Wu Yong. Tong Guan had been so thoroughly defeated that his courage failed and his heart shattered; he feared them even in his dreams, and two-thirds of his great army had been lost. Wu Yong said, “When Tong Guan returns to the capital and reports to the emperor, how could they fail to raise another army against us? We must send someone straight to the Eastern Capital to learn the true state of affairs, return and report to the stronghold, so that we may prepare in advance.” Song Jiang said, “Your counsel, Strategist, accords perfectly with my own thoughts. Which of our brothers would dare undertake the mission?” At once, one man among those seated answered, “I am willing to go.” Everyone looked at him and said, “He is indeed the man for the task; he will surely accomplish something of great consequence.”

p.src: Had this man not gone, there would have been no occasion for stratagems to be laid anew and the government army to suffer another defeat; nor for a charger to perish beneath the verdant peaks in a charge, and a boat sporting on the waves to founder among green reeds. But who from Liangshan Marsh went to gather intelligence? Listen to the next chapter to learn the answer.
